properties.state: {"decision":"DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-02, option 3 of three: the sweep is everything the version-control system tracks, minus NAMED exclusions echoed back with the rule that excluded them. No vocabulary change, no new property, no new node type — so the schema stamp does not move, which on this project is what locks out older binaries. (The node id says `declared` because that was the QUESTION; the answer is `derived`. Kept as a stable handle rather than re-minted, since `cap:coverage` is already GOVERNED_BY it.) ANTHONY'S REASONING, WHICH CORRECTS THE WEAKNESS THIS OPTION WAS RECORDED WITH. The objection on file was that deriving from a repo 'says nothing for a design whose subject is a fleet, a document set, or hardware', against `req:design-anything`. That conflated two different things. THE SUBJECT SYSTEM and THE DESIGN'S ARTIFACTS ARE NOT THE SAME THING, and a sweep only ever covers the second. A satellite, a building, a fleet cannot live in a repo — but its drawings, specs, models, analyses and requirement documents can, and normally do. In his words: 'while a hardware system, for example, can't live within a git repo, its design artifacts can. obviously, for all non-code projects, this is the case.' So the derived scope is not a code-only convenience; it is the general case, and it is MORE clearly right for hardware than for software, because there the artifacts are all there is to sweep. CODE IS THE SPECIAL CASE, NOT THE NORM — and it is special by being MORE than the norm, not less: 'code based projects are the system and can be inspected by the agent as well as the design'. For a codebase the repo holds the subject system AND the design artifacts at once, so a sweep sees both; for everything else it sees the artifacts, which is all a coverage question ever asked about. He also expects that exceptional case to be the majority of reflow2's use, which is why it must not be mistaken for the rule the design is built on. WHAT THIS GENUINELY CANNOT DO, which is a different limitation from the one it was charged with: a design artifact that is NOT under version control — a CAD file on someone's machine, a spec in a wiki, a drawing inside a PLM system — is invisible to a derived sweep. That is not fatal, because the seam already answers it: `coverage_report` takes caller-supplied observations, so an agent that can reach a PLM or a document store sweeps it and hands the paths over exactly as it hands over a repo listing. Derivation is the DEFAULT, not a restriction on what may be observed. WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND WAS NEVER THIS: `cap:coverage` records that the sweep is not persisted, so `detect_gaps` cannot raise coverage from graph state the way `unresolved_drift` is raised from a recorded `DriftEvent`. That deferral survives this decision untouched — it was never the fix for the blind quadrant, and it still needs a node to record a sweep in and a staleness rule (the `cap:freshness` precedent).","name":"Coverage scope is DERIVED from version control — because a sweep covers the design's artifacts, never the subject system","rationale":"Anthony's word, given 2026-08-02 in answer to the three shapes put to him. Recorded with his argument rather than just his choice, because the argument is the part that would otherwise be lost: it is not merely a preference between three costs, it identifies an ERROR in how option 3 was described to him — the artifact/subject conflation — and that error is what would have made a later reader re-open a settled question. The two rejected shapes are kept in the record deliberately (ADR discipline): (1) a scope property on Project/Component, cheap but with no history and nowhere to date a sweep; (2) a first-class node recording a sweep and its scope, which would have closed the persistence deferral in the same move but costs a schema change and pulls in the staleness decision. Both remain available as an OVERRIDE for a subject version control cannot enumerate — this decision fixes the default, not the ceiling.","status":"accepted"}
